author: Ada Offonry
text:
After twenty years of hiring quants and engineers for hedge funds and investment banks, I've come to realise that although job titles are useful, they do not tell the full story of your scope, skills and impact.

The same work carries different labels at different firms. For example, a platform engineer at one fund is an infrastructure engineer at the next and a production engineer at the one after that, even though the responsibilities barely change.

Some ML hires did not have ML in their title before getting those roles. They were backend engineers shipping inference pipelines or infrastructure engineers running GPU clusters.

So before you discount a job because of the title, read the job description properly:

 ➡️ What does this person own day to day
 ➡️ Which systems and tools are named
 ➡️ What has to be true for them to succeed in the first year

Then match your experience against that.

If the responsibilities look familiar, chances are you are qualified enough to apply.

author: Sophie Kay
text:
I'm not an engineering recruiter by trade

But Staffr encompasses your entire hiring stack - GTM & Tech

And even in the 24 months building Staffr & learning about the other side of the coin 

It's clear even to me that engineering hiring at AI startups has completely changed in the last 12 months alone

18 months ago, the brief was simple - find strong engineers who can move fast

Now the conversations are completely different & I think Ryan Davies would agree with me here

Founders are asking for Engineers who understand AI/ML at a product level, not just tooling, people who can build with AI, not just integrate APIs on top of existing architecture, full-stack engineers who can own end-to-end (leaner teams, higher output expected from each person), strong opinions on system design in an era where models are doing more of the execution

The candidate who was a 9/10 18 months ago might be a 6/10 today if they haven't been building in this environment

And the salaries? They have shifted, FAST

Senior engineers at AI-native startups in London, SF or NYC are now looking at packages that would have been Series B+ numbers two years ago

The companies winning the engineering talent right now are moving quickly and offering slick equity

Sell your MISSION, not just the role

author: Shourya Marwaha
text:
After sending over 150 job applications as a data scientist, I noticed something nobody really talks about openly.

The role has quietly changed. The job descriptions haven't caught up.
Three years ago a data scientist job asked for Python, SQL, some machine learning knowledge, and the ability to present findings clearly. That was the standard package.

Now I open the same job title and see Docker, Kubernetes, MLflow, Airflow, CI/CD pipelines, cloud deployment on AWS or GCP, LLM integration, RAG architecture, vector databases, and prompt engineering. Sometimes all in the same posting for a mid-level role.

Companies aren't just hiring data scientists anymore. They want someone who can build the model, deploy it, monitor it in production, connect it to an LLM, and explain the results to a non-technical stakeholder by Friday afternoon.
The research backs this up. Demand for NLP skills in data science job postings jumped from 5% in 2024 to 19% in 2025. MLOps knowledge is now expected, not optional. AI and LLM familiarity appear in nearly a quarter of all data scientist job ads right now.

The honest version of what companies want in 2026 is a data scientist who thinks like an ML engineer and communicates like a business analyst. That combination is genuinely rare and that's exactly where the opportunity sits.

I have been building MLOps and AI skills deliberately over the past few months because of this shift. Not because a course told me to but because the job market made it obvious. And the more I learn the more I realise these skills make you genuinely more useful, not just more hireable.

If you are studying data science right now the curriculum worth following is not just models and statistics. It is models, deployment, monitoring, and LLMs together. The gap between those two paths is where careers are being won or lost right now.

author: Yuliia Vydysh
text:
Anatomy of a premature AI hire:

A while back, I helped a Seed client place a brilliant ML specialist. He was highly skilled but instantly lonely.

Turns out, "specialist" only means something if there’s a team around you to specialize alongside. Without one, you're just a guy in a vacuum.

Month 1: He improved model latency to perfection.

Month 2: When asked to ship, he pointed out that the model wasn't wired to a data pipeline, evals, or UI, because none of those existed yet.

Month 3: He was bored and fine-tuning the doorknob of a house with no walls.

The founder spent their nights gluing the rest of the stack together while their top specialist waited for "actual ML work."

(Unless your product is the foundation model itself, hiring extreme niche depth on Seed is one of the easiest ways to burn your runway).

And we couldn't blame the candidate - he wasn't a bad hire. We just confused "narrow domain expertise" with "someone who can actually ship an end-to-end feature."

If you hire the first engineer in the room, you need someone to wire the data and build the house. 

Leave a specialist title for the good times.

Who else has hired depth when you desperately needed width?

✅ Micro-segmentation to contain lateral movement

author: Thibault GEOUI, PhD
text:
𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐫 𝐀𝐈 𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐬 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐛𝐢𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐲 𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐛𝐞 𝐛𝐫𝐮𝐭𝐞-𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐚𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐞. 𝐒𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐬, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐛𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐚𝐬 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐦𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐬. The real question is whether they will bring scientists in as partners, or extract their expertise as just another dataset.

A few years ago we build a platform to make sense of messy life-science data. We staffed it with strong engineers, many from banking. It did not work. The data was pharmacology and chemistry, and the difficulty was never the volume, it was that the same thing gets named a dozen ways and you need a subject-matter expert to read through the mess. We eventually rebalanced the team. I have since heard the identical story from inside a large tech company: hire technologists, stall, hire scientists, recover.

That correction is now happening at industry scale, and it shows up in the hiring data. Google DeepMind is recruiting a virologist for biosecurity work, wet-lab BSL-3 experience required, at a package no academic lab could match. Anthropic and OpenAI are hiring experimental and computational biologists. NVIDIA wants digital-biology researchers. Techbios like Recursion, Insilico Medicine, insitro and Isomorphic Labs were built bilingual from day one.

The part almost nobody is discussing sits underneath all of that. There is now a market for biology and chemistry PhDs to train and grade frontier AI models on contract, through intermediaries like Mercor, Handshake and Alignerr, at $65 to $300 an hour. This is the high-skill extension of the data-labeling economy

Karen Hao documents in Empire of AI, moved from low-wage annotators in Nairobi to credentialed experts in expensive cities. The tell is the same in both: the listing names the staffing firm, almost never the lab whose model you are actually improving.

The hiring is the easy part. Putting a medicinal chemist and an ML engineer in the same room and getting them to respect each other is the hard part, and I have watched that fail more than once. There is an asymmetry nobody prices in: a scientist can learn to code on a laptop, but you cannot become a bench scientist without a lab and years of tacit craft, yet inside these companies a scientist who cannot code is often the one sidelined.

I wrote the long version, with the numbers, the six clusters of who is hiring, and a falsifiable prediction about where these roles drift in eighteen months 👇

I've reviewed many AI job postings across both local and international markets, and one pattern keeps appearing.

Many companies advertise for an AI Engineer, but the role combines responsibilities from Machine Learning Engineering, Data Science, Research Engineering, MLOps, Backend Engineering, Data Engineering, AI Platform Engineering, Prompt Engineering, and Generative AI Engineering into a single position.

The result?
Both employers and candidates end up with different expectations of what an AI Engineer is actually does.

Here's the reality.

Machine Learning Engineering and AI Engineering are closely related, but they are not the same discipline.

A Machine Learning Engineer typically focuses on data, model training, optimization, deployment, and ML pipelines.

A modern AI Engineer is more focused on building intelligent products using foundation models through RAG, AI Agents, Context Engineering, Tool Integrations, Memory Systems, Evaluation Frameworks, Guardrails, LLMOps, and production AI applications.

These are different engineering challenges, even though they overlap.
Another issue is the experience requirement.

Many job descriptions ask for 5 to 8+ years of AI Engineering experience, while much of today's GenAI ecosystem, including LLM applications and agent frameworks, has only matured within the last few years.

Experience absolutely matters.
But it should be measured by the systems you've built, the production problems you've solved, and the engineering decisions you've made, not simply by the number of years attached to a technology label.

I also see many resumes listing:
• ChatGPT
• Gemini
• Claude
• OpenAI
under the Skills section.

These are models and platforms, not engineering skills.

The real skills are:
• Software Engineering
• System Design
• Problem Solving
• AI Architecture
• Context Engineering
• RAG
• Agentic Systems
• Vector Search
• LLM Evaluation
• Production Deployment
• Performance Optimization

Frameworks will change.
Models will evolve.
APIs will be replaced.
Strong engineering fundamentals remain valuable.

Job descriptions should focus on the business problems engineers are expected to solve, not on a checklist of every trending AI framework.
Likewise, candidates should focus less on collecting tool names and more on demonstrating their ability to build reliable, scalable, production-ready AI systems.

As the AI industry matures, clearer role definitions and better hiring standards will benefit everyone.

Companies will hire better.
Engineers will prepare better.
And we'll build better AI products.

Have you noticed the same gap between AI job descriptions and the actual work being done?

author: Misha Zahid
text:
Not every AI problem needs the same person.

Hiring the wrong level for the job is why most "AI initiatives" either stall or overspend. Here's the breakdown I use to explain it to founders and teams:

Data Analyst  You need to understand what's happening. They turn raw data into clear dashboards and reports. Fast, affordable, and the right starting point before you build anything predictive.

ML Engineer  You need to predict or automate something. They build, train, and deploy an actual working model into your workflow not just a proof of concept sitting in a notebook.

AI & Data Strategist  You need AI to become a real competitive advantage. They shape the roadmap, align models with business strategy, and build decision infrastructure that compounds over time.

Most companies jump straight to hiring a strategist when they actually need an analyst first. Or they hire an analyst and expect strategist-level outcomes.
Match the partner to the goal, not the hype.

Save this the next time you're deciding who to bring in.

author: Shashikkanth Singapuram
text:
The talent market for Data Engineers in India is quietly becoming the tightest it's ever been.

Everyone talks about AI/ML talent. Fewer people are talking about the infrastructure layer underneath it.

You can't run production ML without clean, reliable data pipelines and the engineers who know how to build them at scale are increasingly rare and increasingly expensive.

What's driving this:
- Every AI initiative at every funded startup needs a data foundation first
- Senior Data Engineers who've worked on high-throughput real-time systems are genuinely scarce
- Big tech companies have retained most of the best ones with comp that startups can't easily match

Current market reality: 
- Senior Data Engineer (5+ years, real-time pipeline experience): 35+ LPA 
- Staff / Principal Data Engineer (8+ years, architecture ownership): 60+ LPA

If you're building an AI product and you haven't invested in your data infrastructure team, the models won't save you.

Are you finding this in your own hiring?
